full_name: Prince's Golf Club (Shore and Dunes nines)

summary.text: Prince's is a 27-hole links at Sandwich in Kent, and this round pairs the Shore and Dunes nines.

setting.text: A links course running along the south-east Kent coastline.
The Shore and Dunes combination is the main 18-hole layout at Prince's, according to Top100golfcourses.

history.text: Built by Charles Hutchings, the 1902 Amateur Champion, on land donated by the Earl of Guilford, and finished late in 1906.
Financed by Sir Harry Mallaby-Deeley and his friend Percy Montagu Lucas, who became the club's first Secretary.
The original course was the first designed to counter the new Haskell ball and ran to just under 7,000 yards.
A. J. Balfour, the former Prime Minister, drove the first ball as Club Captain in the Founder's Vase in June 1907.

In the First World War the links became a coastal defence and training area. The first secretary, Percy Lucas, kept the greens cut, and soldiers billeted in the clubhouse gave Percy's son his nickname, 'Laddie'.
In the Second World War the course was all but obliterated. Lord Brabazon likened its use for target practice to 'throwing darts at a Rembrandt'.
Australian property developer Sir Aynsley Bridgland rescued it after the war. Sir Guy Campbell and John Morrison redesigned the course in 1950 into 27 holes, with no blind tee or approach shots.
The present three nines, Shore, Dunes and Himalayas, each start and finish beside the clubhouse. The central clubhouse opened in 1985, opened by Peter Alliss.
The club hosted the 1932 Open Championship, won by Gene Sarazen with a then record low score of 283, five ahead of Macdonald Smith.

Sarazen used his newly invented sand iron at the 1932 Open. The bunker beside the 9th green on the Himalayas nine, one he played from on his way to victory, was named the Sarazen Bunker by Padraig Harrington in June 2011.
Prince's is the only club to have hosted The Open just once.

Other events hosted include the 1956 Curtis Cup, the 2006 Amateur Championship and the 2013 Amateur Championship (the 2013 one co-hosted with Royal Cinque Ports). The 2030 Walker Cup is scheduled for Prince's.
The 1954 Dunlop Masters, won by Bobby Locke, was the first major event on the post-war layout.
The McGuirk family own the club and have used Martin Ebert's architecture firm to update the course, according to a Golf Chronicle review quoted by the club.

trivia.text: Each of the three nines is par 36: Shore 3,419 yards, Dunes 3,436 yards, Himalayas 3,376 yards.
Phil Mickelson and Gary Player are honorary life members.
Henry Cotton, playing the 1932 Open with a high fever and fortified by champagne, finished on 295. He won his first Open two years later at the neighbouring Royal St George's.
James Braid, then 62 and a five-time Open winner, failed to qualify for the 1932 Open at Prince's.
Top100golfcourses' 2015 Kent county ranking placed the Shore and Dunes combination 3rd in Kent, behind Royal St George's and Royal Cinque Ports.
Top100golfcourses added the Himalayas nine to its Kent Top 25 at number 23 in 2015, the first time it had listed a nine-hole course separately at a 27-hole facility.

local.text: Prince's sits immediately next to Royal St George's and on the same stretch of coast as Royal Cinque Ports, near Sandwich in Kent.
The original clubhouse, now a hotel called The Lodge (opened May 2012), stands by the entrance next to the 14th tee of Royal St George's.

WWII pilot and MP Laddie Lucas was born in the old clubhouse. After his Spitfire was crippled over northern France he made an emergency landing at Prince's, marked by a plaque by the 4th tee on the Himalayas nine.
